lines.text: Three words saved the euro: whatever it takes.

lines.text: In the summer of 2012, a currency shared by hundreds of millions of people looked like it might break apart.
lines.say: In the summer of 2012, a currency shared by hundreds of millions of people looked like it might break apart.

lines.text: Today, more than 357 million people use the euro, in 21 countries.
lines.say: Today, more than three hundred fifty-seven million people use the euro, in twenty-one countries.

lines.text: So in this video: why Europe built one money, why it's so hard to run, and how it reaches your wallet in America.

lines.text: Chapter one: why build one money?
lines.say: Chapter one: why build one money?

lines.text: Picture Europe in the 1980s. Germany had the mark, France the franc, Italy the lira.
lines.say: Picture Europe in the 1980s. Germany had the mark, France the franc, Italy the lira.

lines.text: Every trip and every trade across a border meant swapping money and paying fees.
lines.say: Every trip and every trade across a border meant swapping money and paying fees.

lines.text: And when currencies swung, a company's profit could vanish on the exchange rate alone.
lines.say: And when currencies swung, a company's profit could vanish on the exchange rate alone.

lines.text: Leaders also wanted to tie the continent together after a century of wars. Money was part of that plan.
lines.say: Leaders also wanted to tie the continent together after a century of wars. Money was part of that plan.

lines.text: Europe had tried tying currencies together before. In 1992, traders forced the British pound out of that system in a single day.
lines.say: Europe had tried tying currencies together before. In nineteen ninety-two, traders forced the British pound out of that system in a single day.

lines.text: A single currency was meant to end that kind of attack for good. You can't bet against a currency that no longer exists.
lines.say: A single currency was meant to end that kind of attack for good. You can't bet against a currency that no longer exists.

lines.text: In 1992, they signed the Maastricht Treaty, which set the rules for joining.
lines.say: In 1992, they signed the Maastricht Treaty, which set the rules for joining.

lines.text: Two famous ones: a budget deficit no bigger than 3% of GDP, and government debt no bigger than 60%.
lines.say: Two famous ones: a budget deficit no bigger than three percent of G D P, and government debt no bigger than sixty percent.

lines.text: The UK negotiated an opt-out and kept the pound.
lines.say: The UK negotiated an opt-out and kept the pound.

lines.text: On January 1, 1999, the euro launched in 11 countries, at first only on screens and in bank accounts.
lines.say: On January first, nineteen ninety-nine, the euro launched in eleven countries, at first only on screens and in bank accounts.

lines.text: Notes and coins arrived on January 1, 2002, in 12 countries, after Greece joined.
lines.say: Notes and coins arrived on January first, two thousand two, in twelve countries, after Greece joined.

lines.text: Each country locked in a conversion rate. One euro was set at 1.95583 German marks.
lines.say: Each country locked in a conversion rate. One euro was set at one point nine five five eight three German marks.

lines.text: The club kept growing. Bulgaria became the 21st member on January 1, 2026.
lines.say: The club kept growing. Bulgaria became the twenty-first member on January first, twenty twenty-six.

lines.text: Not every EU country uses it, though. Denmark has an opt-out, and Sweden and Poland still use their own money.
lines.say: Not every EU country uses it, though. Denmark has an opt-out, and Sweden and Poland still use their own money.

lines.text: And one central bank in Frankfurt, the European Central Bank, took charge of interest rates for all of them.
lines.say: And one central bank in Frankfurt, the European Central Bank, took charge of interest rates for all of them.

lines.text: Chapter two: why it's so hard to run.
lines.say: Chapter two: why it's so hard to run.

lines.text: Here's the core problem. Twenty-one economies share one interest rate.
lines.say: Here's the core problem. Twenty-one economies share one interest rate.

lines.text: If Germany is booming and another country is in a slump, one rate can't be right for both.
lines.say: If Germany is booming and another country is in a slump, one rate can't be right for both.

lines.text: A booming country wants higher rates to cool down. A struggling one wants lower rates to recover.
lines.say: A booming country wants higher rates to cool down. A struggling one wants lower rates to recover.

lines.text: Problem two: no exchange rate to adjust.
lines.say: Problem two: no exchange rate to adjust.

lines.text: Before the euro, a struggling country's currency could fall, making its exports cheaper and helping it recover.
lines.say: Before the euro, a struggling country's currency could fall, making its exports cheaper and helping it recover.

lines.text: Inside the euro, that escape hatch is gone. The only way to get cheaper is slower wages and prices, which is painful.
lines.say: Inside the euro, that escape hatch is gone. The only way to get cheaper is slower wages and prices, which is painful.

lines.text: Problem three: no shared budget.
lines.say: Problem three: no shared budget.

lines.text: In the US, when one state has a bad year, federal money for things like unemployment benefits and Social Security still flows in.
lines.say: In the US, when one state has a bad year, federal money for things like unemployment benefits and Social Security still flows in.

lines.text: The euro area shares a currency, but each country mostly runs its own budget and borrows on its own.
lines.say: The euro area shares a currency, but each country mostly runs its own budget and borrows on its own.

lines.text: Economists have a name for this: an optimal currency area. A shared currency works best when workers can move easily and budgets are shared.
lines.say: Economists have a name for this: an optimal currency area. A shared currency works best when workers can move easily and budgets are shared.

lines.text: But moving for a job across Europe often means a new language and new rules, so that safety valve is weaker.
lines.say: But moving for a job across Europe often means a new language and new rules, so that safety valve is weaker.

lines.text: In the 2000s, lenders treated Greek or Spanish government debt almost like German debt, so borrowing got cheap everywhere.
lines.say: In the 2000s, lenders treated Greek or Spanish government debt almost like German debt, so borrowing got cheap everywhere.

lines.text: That cheap money helped fuel housing booms in places like Spain and Ireland.
lines.say: That cheap money helped fuel housing booms in places like Spain and Ireland.

lines.text: That combination worked fine in good times. Then the good times ended.
lines.say: That combination worked fine in good times. Then the good times ended.

lines.text: Chapter three: the crisis.
lines.say: Chapter three: the crisis.

lines.text: In October 2009, a new Greek government revealed its deficit was far bigger than reported.
lines.say: In October two thousand nine, a new Greek government revealed its deficit was far bigger than reported.

lines.text: Lenders panicked, and Greece's borrowing costs shot up.
lines.say: Lenders panicked, and Greece's borrowing costs shot up.

lines.text: Greek government debt went from about 105% of GDP in 2007 to about 175% by 2011.
lines.say: Greek government debt went from about a hundred five percent of G D P in two thousand seven to about a hundred seventy-five percent by twenty eleven.

lines.text: In May 2010, Europe and the IMF agreed a first bailout of 110 billion euros. Two more followed, in 2012 and 2015.
lines.say: In May twenty ten, Europe and the I M F agreed a first bailout of a hundred ten billion euros. Two more followed, in twenty twelve and twenty fifteen.

lines.text: Ireland and Portugal needed rescue loans too, and later Spain's banks and Cyprus.
lines.say: Ireland and Portugal needed rescue loans too, and later Spain's banks and Cyprus.

lines.text: By March 2012, Greece's 10-year bond yield was above 40%. That's what lenders demanded to lend for a decade.

lines.text: And the fear spread. Investors worried Spain and Italy could be next, and that the euro itself might split.
lines.say: And the fear spread. Investors worried Spain and Italy could be next, and that the euro itself might split.

lines.text: That's when Mario Draghi, head of the ECB, gave his speech in London on July 26, 2012.
lines.say: That's when Mario Draghi, head of the E C B, gave his speech in London on July twenty-sixth, twenty twelve.

lines.text: The message was simple: the central bank would stand behind the euro's government bonds, within its rules.

lines.text: Borrowing costs for Spain and Italy began to ease, and the panic faded.

lines.text: But Greece's debt kept climbing as its economy shrank, peaking around 210% of GDP in 2020.

lines.text: Chapter four: running the euro today.
lines.say: Chapter four: running the euro today.

lines.text: After the crisis, the ECB went to extremes. In June 2014, it pushed its deposit rate below zero.

lines.text: Banks actually paid to park money there, and rates stayed negative until July 2022.
lines.say: Banks actually paid to park money there, and rates stayed negative until July twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: Then inflation exploded after energy prices spiked, hitting 10.6% in the euro area in October 2022.
lines.say: Then inflation exploded after energy prices spiked, hitting ten point six percent in the euro area in October twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: The ECB raised its deposit rate all the way to 4% by September 2023, then cut it to 2% by June 2025.

lines.text: In 2026, energy prices jumped again. Euro area inflation was 3.2% in August 2026, with energy up 14.3%.

lines.text: So in September 2026, the ECB raised its deposit rate to 2.5%.
lines.say: So in September twenty twenty-six, the E C B raised its deposit rate to two and a half percent.

lines.text: That's the one-rate problem again. Countries hit hardest by energy prices and slower growth all get the same higher rate.

lines.text: To stop one country's borrowing costs from spiraling again, the ECB created a new backstop tool in July 2022.
lines.say: To stop one country's borrowing costs from spiraling again, the E C B created a new backstop tool in July twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: And the debt rules still bite. Euro area government debt was 87.8% of GDP at the end of 2025, well above the 60% target.

lines.text: Each country still runs its own budget, so every downturn reopens the same argument about who pays.

lines.text: Think cars, medicines, machinery, and wine. A stronger euro tends to make them pricier in dollars, and a weaker euro, cheaper.

lines.text: Europe built the euro to end currency swaps, steady trade, and tie the continent together.

post.yt_desc:
The euro launched in 1999 and today more than 357 million people in 21 countries use it. This video explains why Europe built one money, why sharing one interest rate without a shared budget makes it so hard to run, how the Greek debt crisis nearly broke it until Mario Draghi's 'whatever it takes' speech in July 2012, and how the euro-dollar exchange rate reaches American travelers, importers and investors.
